response.answer: To reproduce an end-to-end experiment, deliver the GitHub repository at https://github.com/iterative/example-get-started-experiments, which includes a DVC pipeline and a Jupyter notebook. Use `dvc pull` to download data and `dvc exp run` to execute the pipeline.

results.content: dvc.org/doc/start/experiment-management/experiments. # DVC Get Started: Experiments. This is an auto-generated repository for use in DVC Get Started: Experiments. This DVC project comes with a preconfigured DVC remote storage that holds raw data (input), intermediate, and final results that are produced. You can run `dvc pull` to download the data:. Run `dvc exp run` to reproduce the pipeline:. dvc exp runData and pipelines are up to date. If you'd like to test commands like `dvc push`, that require write access to the remote storage, the easiest way would be to set up a "local remote" on your file system:. > This kind of remote is located in the local file system, but is external to the DVC project. Contains an end-to-end Jupyter notebook that loads data, trains a model and reports model performance. Contains a DVC pipeline `dvc.yaml` that was created by refactoring the above notebook into individual pipeline stages. The pipeline artifacts (processed data, model file, etc) are automatically versioned. This tag also contains a GitHub Actions workflow that reruns the pipeline if any changes are introduced to the pipeline-related files. CML is used in this workflow to provision a cloud-based GPU machine as well as report model performance results in Pull Requests. The data files, DVC files, and results change as stages are created one by one. After cloning and using `dvc pull` to download data, models, and plots tracked by DVC, the workspace should look like this:. # <-- Directory with raw and intermediate data│ ├── pool_data # <-- Raw image data│ ├── pool_data.dvc # <-- .dvc file - a placeholder/pointer to raw data│ ├── test_data # <-- Processed test data│ └── train_data # <-- Processed train data├── dvc.lock├── dvc.yaml # <-- DVC pipeline file ├── models│ └── model.pkl # <-- Trained model file ├── notebooks│ └── TrainSegModel.ipynb # <-- Initial notebook (refactored into `dvc.yaml`) ├── params.yaml # <-- Parameters file├── requirements.txt # <-- Python dependencies needed in the project├── results # <-- DVCLive reports and plots │ ├── evaluate │ └── train└── src # <-- Source code to run the pipeline stages ├── data_split.py ├── evaluate.py └── train.py. dvc.org/doc/start/experiment-management/experiments. python machine-learning computer-vision reproducible-research example reproducibility dvc.

results.content:
Title: From Jupyter Notebook to DVC pipeline for reproducible ML experiments – DVC
# From Jupyter Notebook to DVC pipeline for reproducible ML experiments. In this guide, we will explore an intermediate step: use Papermill to build a one-stage DVC pipeline that executes our entire notebook. Stages in a DVC pipeline consist of commands as we could run them in our own terminal. To start experimenting with our pipeline, we need to parameterize our notebook. With our parameterized notebook in place, we can create our pipeline with DVC. $ dvc stage add -n run_notebook -d notebooks/pokemon_classifier.ipynb -d data/external/images-gen-1-8 -d data/external/stats/pokemon-gen-1-8.csv -o data/processed/pokemon -o data/processed/pokemon.csv -o data/processed/pokemon-with-image-paths.csv -o outputs/model.pckl -o outputs/confusion_matrix.png -o outputs/train_history.png -M outputs/metrics.yaml papermill notebooks/pokemon_classifier.ipynb outputs/pokemon_classifier_out.ipynb. stages: run_notebook: cmd: > papermill notebooks/pokemon_classifier.ipynb outputs/pokemon_classifier_out.ipynb deps: - notebooks/pokemon_classifier.ipynb - data/external/images-gen-1-8 - data/external/stats/pokemon-gen-1-8.csv outs: - data/processed/pokemon - data/processed/pokemon.csv - data/processed/pokemon-with-image-paths.csv - outputs/model.pckl - outputs/confusion_matrix.png - outputs/train_history.png metrics: - outputs/metrics.yaml: cache: false. We can run the pipeline with the `dvc repro` command, and DVC will execute our notebook. stages: run_notebook: cmd: > papermill notebooks/pokemon_classifier.ipynb outputs/pokemon_classifier_out.ipynb + -p SEED ${base.seed} + -p POKEMON_TYPE_TRAIN ${base.pokemon_type_train} + -p SOURCE_DIRECTORY ${data_preprocess.source_directory} + -p DESTINATION_DIRECTORY ${data_preprocess.destination_directory} + -p TRAIN_DATA_IMAGES ${data_preprocess.dataset_images} + -p TRAIN_DATA_LABELS ${data_preprocess.dataset_labels} + -p MODEL_TEST_SIZE ${train.test_size} + -p MODEL_LEARNING_RATE ${train.learning_rate} + -p MODEL_EPOCHS ${train.epochs} + -p MODEL_BATCH_SIZE ${train.batch_size} deps: - notebooks/pokemon_classifier.ipynb - data/external/images-gen-1-8 - data/external/stats/pokemon-gen-1-8.csv outs: - data/processed/pokemon - data/processed/pokemon.csv - data/processed/pokemon-with-image-paths.csv - outputs/model.pckl - outputs/confusion_matrix.png - outputs/train_history.png metrics: - outputs/metrics.yaml: cache: false. That means we now have the reproducible pipeline we set out to create: we can go back to any experiment and get the precise combination of code, data, parameters, and results. We can use `dvc exp run` to run an experiment after we have changed the parameters in `params.yaml`, or we could change the parameters in the command itself with the `-S` option. Throughout this guide, we transformed a Jupyter Notebook into a codified pipeline for reproducible experiments. We used Papermill to parameterize our notebook so that we could run it with a single command and then created a pipeline in DVC to run that command for us. With our DVC pipeline tracking and versioning every experiment, we can discover which combination of code, data, and parameters provides the best results.

results.content: # From Jupyter Notebook to DVC pipeline for reproducible ML experiments. DVC can help us with this, but converting a notebook into a complete pipeline may seem a bit daunting. In this guide, we will explore an intermediate step: use Papermill to build a one-stage DVC pipeline that executes our entire notebook. We will then use our pipeline to run and version ML experiments. Its ease of use makes it the perfect tool for prototyping, usually resulting in a script in which we preprocess the data, do a train/test split, train our model, and evaluate it. We can solve our need for reproducibility by transforming our notebook into a codified pipeline with defined inputs and outputs. For the sake of simplicity, we will create a pipeline with just one stage for now: run all of the code in our notebook. With this tool, we can parameterize our notebook and run experiments from our CLI with a single command.

results.content: Published Time: October 24, 2022 From Jupyter Notebook to DVC pipeline for reproducible ML experiments This website stores cookies on your computer. From Jupyter Notebook to DVC pipeline for reproducible ML experiments Jupyter Notebooks are great for prototyping, but eventually we want to move towards reproducible experiments. In this guide, we will explore an intermediate step: use Papermill to build a one-stage DVC pipeline that executes our entire notebook. ### Parameterize notebook While we would technically have a DVC pipeline if we added this command as a stage, its usefulness would be somewhat limited. For example, we change the following section of code like so: estimator = model.fit(X_train, y_train, Now we can run our notebook through Papermill with changed parameters: ### Create DVC pipeline With our parameterized notebook in place, we can create our pipeline with DVC. Lastly, we type in the command that DVC should execute for that stage: -d data/external/images-gen-1-8 \ -d data/external/stats/pokemon-gen-1-8.csv \ -o data/processed/pokemon.csv \ -o data/processed/pokemon-with-image-paths.csv \ papermill notebooks/pokemon_classifier.ipynb outputs/pokemon_classifier_out.ipynb The uppercase `-M` option (as opposed to the lowercase `-m` option) tells DVC not to track the resulting metrics file. We can run the pipeline with the `dvc repro` command, and DVC will execute our notebook. ### Version our data, models, and plots with DVC As we discussed earlier, we want to version every component of our experiments to achieve true reproducibility: code, parameters, data, models, metrics, and plots. That means we now have the reproducible pipeline we set out to create: we can go back to any experiment and get the precise combination of code, data, parameters, and results. We can use `dvc exp run` to run an experiment after we have changed the parameters in `params.yaml`, or we could change the parameters in the command itself with the `-S` option. Throughout this guide, we transformed a Jupyter Notebook into a codified pipeline for reproducible experiments. We used Papermill to parameterize our notebook so that we could run it with a single command and then created a pipeline in DVC to run that command for us. With our DVC pipeline tracking and versioning every experiment, we can discover which combination of code, data, and parameters provides the best results.

results.title: R code and reproducible model development with DVC – DVC
results.content:
Title: R code and reproducible model development with DVC – DVC
# R code and reproducible model development with DVC. DVC or Data Version Control tool — its idea is to track files/data dependencies during model development in order to facilitate reproducibility and track data files versioning. For example, instead of having one big R file with code it is better to split code in several logical files — each responsible for one small piece of work. Every time when a change/commit in some of the codes and data sets is made, DVC will reproduce new results with just one bash command on a linux (or Win environment). ## R example — data and code clarification. We’ll take an Python example from DVC tutorial (written by Dmitry Petrov) and rewrite that code in R. After that we will simulate some changes in the codes and see how DVC works on reproducibility. **evaluate.R** — with trained model we are predicting target on test data set. With code below 5 R scripts with `dvc run` are executed. It is important to use `dvc run` — with this command R script are entering pipeline (DAG graph). $ dvc run Rscript code/parsingxml.R data/Posts.xml data/Posts.csv # Split training and testing dataset. $ dvc run Rscript code/train_test_spliting.R data/Posts.csv 0.33 20170426 data/train_post.csv data/test_post.csv # Extract features from text data. $ dvc run Rscript code/featurization.R data/train_post.csv data/test_post.csv data/matrix_train.txt data/matrix_test.txt # Train ML model out of the training dataset. $ dvc run Rscript code/train_model.R data/matrix_train.txt 20170426 data/glmnet.Rdata # Evaluate the model by the testing dataset. $ dvc run Rscript code/evaluate.R data/glmnet.Rdata data/matrix_test.txt data/evaluation.txt # The result. DVC knows based on DAG graph that changed `train_model.R` file will only change following files: `Glmnet.RData` and `Evaluation.txt`. $ vi train_model.R $ git commit -am "Ridge penalty instead of lasso" $ dvc repro data/evaluation.txt Reproducing run command for data item data/glmnet.Rdata. Args: Rscript code/train_model.R data/matrix_train.txt 20170426 data/glmnet.Rdata Reproducing run command for data item data/evaluation.txt. Args: Rscript code/evaluate.R data/glmnet.Rdata data/matrix_test.txt data/evaluation.txt $ cat data/evaluation.txt "AUC for the test file is : 0.947697381983095". On the R example we saw how DVC memorizes dependency graph and based on that graph re executes only jobs that are related to the latest changes.
